prompt:
A country currently generates 70 percent of its
electricity from coal and natural gas and wants to
reach 90 percent renewable electricity within 15 years.
Develop a detailed transition strategy. Compare solar,
wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, nuclear, battery
storage, pumped hydro, and demand-response
technologies. Analyze technical feasibility, grid
stability, transmission requirements, seasonal energy
storage, land use, supply-chain constraints, workforce
requirements, capital costs, operating costs, energy
security, and environmental impacts. Identify the major
trade-offs and failure modes. Then propose a phased
15-year implementation plan with measurable milestones.
Explain the reasoning behind your recommendations in
detail.

Design a comprehensive strategy for a rapidly growing
city of five million people that expects its population
to increase by 40 percent over the next twenty years.
The city already faces traffic congestion, housing
shortages, aging water systems, electricity demand
growth, air pollution, and limited public funds.
Develop an integrated plan covering transportation,
housing, water, electricity, waste management, public
health, climate resilience, and digital infrastructure.
For each area, analyze competing priorities,
dependencies, risks, costs, and possible unintended
consequences. Explain how the city should sequence
investments over twenty years and how success should be
measured.

A manufacturing company operates twelve factories
across multiple countries and wants to reduce its total
carbon emissions by 80 percent while keeping production
costs competitive. Build a detailed decision framework
for achieving this target. Consider renewable
electricity, electrification of industrial processes,
energy efficiency, alternative fuels, supply-chain
changes, transportation, carbon capture, equipment
replacement cycles, and carbon offsets. Discuss
financial, technical, regulatory, operational, and
supply-chain risks. Compare short-term and long-term
strategies and propose a prioritized implementation
roadmap with clear reasoning.

Imagine that a region experiences a severe five-year
drought while its population and agricultural demand
continue to grow. Develop a detailed water-security
strategy that balances urban consumption, agriculture,
industry, ecosystem protection, and future population
growth. Evaluate desalination, wastewater recycling,
groundwater extraction, reservoirs, conservation, smart
metering, agricultural efficiency, water pricing, and
inter-regional transfers. Analyze economic,
environmental, technical, political, and social
trade-offs. Construct a phased response for immediate
emergency measures, medium-term stabilization, and
long-term resilience.

A national government wants to build a resilient
digital infrastructure strategy for the next fifteen
years. It must support cloud computing, artificial
intelligence, healthcare, banking, government services,
education, and emergency communications while remaining
resilient to cyberattacks, natural disasters,
supply-chain disruptions, and power failures. Develop a
detailed architecture and policy strategy. Compare
centralized and distributed infrastructure, public
cloud, sovereign cloud, edge computing, local data
centers, backup power, network redundancy,
cybersecurity controls, and disaster recovery. Identify
trade-offs and propose measurable resilience targets.

Analyze how a country should prepare its economy and
workforce for widespread adoption of artificial
intelligence and automation over the next twenty years.
Consider productivity, job displacement, creation of
new occupations, education, reskilling, inequality,
taxation, social programs, small businesses, research
investment, cybersecurity, energy demand, and
international competitiveness. Present multiple
plausible future scenarios rather than assuming a
single outcome. For each scenario, identify major
risks, leading indicators, and policy responses. Finish
with a staged strategy that can adapt as conditions
change.

Design and implement in TypeScript an O(n) algorithm
that accepts an unsorted array of integers and returns:
the length of the longest consecutive sequence, the
sequence itself, and the starting and ending values.
Duplicate values may appear and must not affect the
result. If multiple sequences have the same maximum
length, return the one with the smallest starting
value. Do not sort the input. Explain the algorithm,
prove why its expected time complexity is O(n), analyze
space complexity, discuss edge cases, and provide clean
production-quality TypeScript code followed by at least
eight meaningful test cases.

Design a production-quality TypeScript implementation
of an LRU cache with O(1) average-time get and put
operations. Do not use JavaScript Map insertion order
as the eviction mechanism. Implement the required
hash-map and doubly-linked-list logic explicitly.
Support updating existing keys, capacity one, arbitrary
string keys, and generic values. Explain every major
design decision, identify invariants that must remain
true, analyze time and space complexity, discuss common
implementation bugs, and provide a comprehensive test
suite covering eviction, updates, repeated access, and
edge cases.

You are designing a task scheduler in TypeScript. Each
task has an ID, execution duration, and zero or more
dependency IDs. Design an algorithm that validates the
dependency graph, detects cycles, produces a valid
execution order when possible, and calculates the
earliest possible completion time assuming an unlimited
number of workers and that a task can start only after
all dependencies finish. Explain the graph
representation, cycle-detection method, topological
ordering, dynamic-programming step, complexity, and
failure cases. Then provide complete TypeScript code
and a set of nontrivial tests.

Design a thread-safe job-processing architecture for a
service that receives up to 50,000 jobs per minute.
Jobs may be retried, workers may crash, duplicate
messages may be delivered, and jobs must never be
considered successfully completed more than once from
the application's perspective. Explain how you would
implement idempotency, retries with exponential
backoff, dead-letter handling, leases or visibility
timeouts, concurrency control, database transactions,
observability, graceful shutdown, and recovery after
failure. Then provide detailed TypeScript pseudocode or
implementation-level code for the core worker loop and
explain race conditions that must be prevented.

Implement in TypeScript a function that receives
millions of time intervals represented as start and end
integer timestamps and returns the merged
non-overlapping intervals, total covered duration,
largest uncovered gap between the minimum and maximum
timestamps, and maximum number of simultaneously active
intervals. Clearly define how touching intervals and
zero-length intervals are handled. Develop an efficient
algorithm, analyze its time and space complexity,
explain alternative approaches for very large datasets
that do not fit into memory, and provide
production-quality code with extensive edge-case tests.

A Node.js API has gradually become slow under load.
Requests perform authentication, query PostgreSQL, call
two external services, transform large JSON objects,
and publish an event. At 50 requests per second latency
is 120 ms, but at 500 requests per second p95 latency
exceeds 8 seconds and memory continually increases.
Develop a systematic debugging and optimization plan.
Reason about event-loop blocking, connection pools,
unbounded concurrency, memory leaks, garbage
collection, database indexes, N+1 queries, HTTP
connection reuse, timeouts, retries, queues, caching,
backpressure, and instrumentation. Include concrete
TypeScript/Node.js examples showing how you would
restructure the most likely bottlenecks.

Write a detailed educational guide explaining how
modern electrical power grids work for a reader with no
engineering background. Cover electricity generation,
transformers, high-voltage transmission, substations,
distribution networks, frequency and voltage control,
supply-demand balancing, grid operators,
renewable-energy integration, battery storage,
blackouts, and grid restoration. Organize the answer
with clear headings, use practical examples and
analogies, define technical terms when first
introduced, and finish with a concise summary of the
entire electricity journey from power plant to
household.

Create a comprehensive beginner-friendly explanation of
how a web application works from the moment a user
enters a URL until the requested page appears. Explain
DNS, IP addresses, TCP, TLS, HTTP, browsers, CDNs, load
balancers, reverse proxies, web servers, APIs,
application servers, databases, caches, cookies,
authentication, JavaScript execution, rendering, and
browser storage. Follow the request chronologically and
clearly explain which component is responsible for each
stage. Include a realistic example involving a user
signing into an online store.

Write a structured technical guide comparing relational
databases and document databases. Explain schemas,
tables, documents, relationships, normalization,
denormalization, indexes, transactions, ACID
properties, consistency, horizontal and vertical
scaling, replication, sharding, query patterns, data
integrity, and operational complexity. Use PostgreSQL
and MongoDB as concrete examples without presenting
either as universally superior. Include several
application scenarios and explain which characteristics
should influence the database choice in each scenario.

Explain the complete machine-learning lifecycle to a
software developer who understands programming but has
never built a machine-learning system. Cover problem
definition, data collection, cleaning, labeling,
exploratory analysis, feature engineering, training and
validation splits, model selection, training,
overfitting, underfitting, evaluation metrics,
deployment, inference, monitoring, drift, retraining,
versioning, privacy, and reproducibility. Use one
consistent practical example throughout the explanation
and clearly distinguish training from inference.

Prepare a detailed incident-response guide for a
software team operating a high-traffic web service.
Explain detection, alert triage, severity
classification, incident command, communication,
diagnosis, mitigation, rollback, feature flags, logs,
metrics, distributed traces, dashboards, database
investigation, external dependency failures, customer
communication, recovery validation, post-incident
review, and preventive actions. Include a realistic
example where an API deployment causes elevated error
rates and database load. Keep the guide practical and
operational.

Write a comprehensive explanation of containerization
and modern application deployment. Begin with the
problems containers solve and explain images,
containers, registries, Dockerfiles, layers, volumes,
networking, environment variables, secrets, resource
limits, health checks, and logging. Then explain how
container orchestration systems schedule and manage
applications, including replicas, rolling deployments,
service discovery, autoscaling, failure recovery, and
persistent storage. Finish by walking through a
realistic deployment of a frontend, API, and database.

A company operates three factories A, B, and C. Factory
A can produce 1,200 units per day at $18 per unit, B
can produce 900 units per day at $21 per unit, and C
can produce 1,500 units per day at $16 per unit. Daily
demand is 3,000 units. However, at least 600 units must
come from B because of a contract, C can operate at no
more than 80 percent capacity because of maintenance,
and using more than 1,000 units from A adds an overtime
cost of $5 for every A unit above 1,000. Determine a
lowest-cost feasible production allocation. Show the
calculations, verify every constraint, calculate total
cost, and explain why shifting production among
factories would or would not reduce the cost.

A company must schedule six projects A through F. Their
durations in days are A=4, B=7, C=3, D=6, E=5, and F=2.
B and C can begin only after A finishes. D requires B.
E requires both B and C. F requires both D and E.
Assume unlimited workers, but no project can begin
before all of its dependencies are complete. Determine
the earliest start and finish time for every project,
identify the critical path, calculate the minimum total
completion time, and then determine what changes if B
takes three additional days. Show the reasoning step by
step.

An online retailer sells a product for $480. The
retailer first applies a 15 percent promotional
discount. A customer then uses a coupon worth 10
percent of the already-discounted price. Shipping costs
$24 unless the price after both discounts is at least
$375, in which case shipping is free. Finally, 13
percent sales tax is applied to the merchandise price
after discounts plus any shipping charge. The
retailer's original cost for the product is $260 and it
pays the shipping charge itself when shipping is free.
Calculate the customer's final payment, the retailer's
gross profit before other expenses, and the effective
percentage discount relative to the original $480
sticker price. Show every calculation and explain the
order of operations.

A data center has a continuous IT load of 600 kW. Its
initial power usage effectiveness, or PUE, is 1.50. An
efficiency project reduces PUE to 1.25 but requires a
$900,000 upfront investment. Electricity costs $0.12
per kWh during the first year and rises by 4 percent at
the beginning of each subsequent year. Assume 8,760
operating hours per year and that the IT load remains
constant. Calculate annual facility energy consumption
before and after the upgrade, first-year energy and
cost savings, and the cumulative nominal
electricity-cost savings over five years. Determine
whether the $900,000 investment has paid back within
five years and estimate when simple payback occurs.
Show all steps and assumptions.

A delivery company has three trucks. Truck A can carry
8 tonnes and costs $140 per trip, Truck B carries 12
tonnes and costs $190 per trip, and Truck C carries 20
tonnes and costs $310 per trip. The company must move
exactly 120 tonnes. At least two trips must use Truck
A, no more than four trips may use Truck C, and the
total number of trips may not exceed ten. Determine a
minimum-cost feasible combination of integer trips for
A, B, and C. Systematically evaluate the constraints,
show the calculations, report total capacity and total
cost, and explain why no cheaper feasible integer
combination exists.

A company is comparing two server systems for a
five-year deployment. System A costs $18,000 initially,
consumes an average of 420 watts, and requires $1,200
annual maintenance. System B costs $26,000 initially,
consumes 250 watts, and requires $700 annual
maintenance. Both run continuously 8,760 hours per
year. Electricity costs $0.15 per kWh in year one and
increases by 5 percent at the start of each following
year. At the end of year five, System A has a resale
value of $2,000 and System B has a resale value of
$4,000. Calculate year-by-year electricity costs,
maintenance costs, total five-year nominal ownership
cost after resale value, the difference between the
systems, and the approximate electricity price at which
their five-year costs would become equal if all other
assumptions stayed unchanged. Show the reasoning
clearly.
